items.context: @david_eng_mba (26.490 seguidores), en inglés: "Cut power prices 90%. A dollar runs an AI chip 10× longer. Once difficulty adjusts, miners still split ~450 new BTC a day. After the next halving, ~225. At $60K a coin, the cap is 21M. At $600K, it’s still 21M. If demand grows, buyers have to make holders a better offer. $BTC" Publicado hace ~1,9 h: 17 likes, 1 respuesta, 1 cita, 1.427 vistas. Tema halving y emisión; calza con las cifras de tu post (~450 a ~225 BTC al día).
items.suggested_text:
The 450 → 225 step matters more than it looks. After the next halving only 3.125% of the 21M will still be left to issue, and the subsidy drops from 3.125 to 1.5625 BTC per block. New coins become a smaller and smaller share of what actually changes hands; the marginal seller is increasingly an existing holder, not a miner.

Cheaper power doesn't change that math. It pulls in more hashrate, difficulty adjusts, and issuance stays on schedule: the cost per coin can fall, the number of coins can't. I laid out the issuance numbers here: https://x.com/ForecastQuant/status/2122747344701501622

Which leaves an odd dynamic: miners compete harder every cycle for a reward that keeps shrinking, and at some point fees have to carry more of the security budget than the subsidy does.
